analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination at work, in housing, and in federally funded programs based on natural hairstyles like braids and locs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2025 with a bipartisan sponsor pair and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The CROWN Act would make it illegal under federal civil rights law to treat someone differently because of their hair texture or hairstyle when that style is commonly associated with a particular race or national origin — for example, locs, cornrows, twists, braids, Bantu knots, or Afros. The protection would cover employment, housing, public accommodations like businesses open to the public, and federally assisted programs, and it would be enforced through the same machinery as the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Fair Housing Act. The bill states that people, particularly those of African descent, have been denied jobs and opportunities over natural hairstyles, and that some federal courts have read existing civil rights laws too narrowly to protect them.
analysis.who_benefits: People — chiefly Black Americans and others of African descent — who wear natural or protective hairstyles and have faced job losses, hiring rejections, school discipline, or housing denial because of them. The bill text cites federal court rulings that let employers discriminate over hairstyles unrelated to job performance, and notes the Armed Forces only dropped its own restrictive grooming policies in 2018 [S3]. Workers would gain the ability to bring discrimination claims under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act; renters and homebuyers under the Fair Housing Act; students and program participants under Title VI [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It makes it illegal to deny someone a job, a promotion, or fair treatment at work because of hair texture or styles like locs, cornrows, twists, braids, Bantu knots, and Afros.
It extends the same protection to federally assisted programs, housing, and public accommodations, so a landlord or business open to the public could not turn someone away over their hair.

It plugs a gap left by federal court rulings that read the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Fair Housing Act, and related laws narrowly, allowing employers to fire or refuse to hire people over hairstyles with no connection to job performance.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, landlords, schools, and businesses that would need to drop grooming rules targeting natural hairstyles and could face discrimination complaints if they keep them. Compliance costs are modest for most, since the bill layers onto existing civil rights enforcement rather than creating a new system [S3].

drawbacks.text: Employers, schools, and landlords would face new legal exposure: any grooming, uniform, or dress policy could be challenged if it affects hairstyles commonly associated with a race or national origin, and businesses would bear the cost of revising policies and defending complaints.

The bill extends civil rights liability into contexts where appearance rules can serve legitimate purposes (safety equipment, food handling, professional dress), and courts would have to work out where a valid neutral policy ends and a discriminatory one begins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and modest in scope: it closes a specific, documented gap in federal civil rights law that costs people jobs, schooling, and housing opportunities because of their hair [S3]. The costs are the standard burden of any anti-discrimination rule: employers, landlords, and schools must adjust policies, and some marginal disputes will end up in court. The bill does not create a new enforcement agency; it uses the enforcement machinery of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Fair Housing Act, which keeps added bureaucracy low [S3]. The main weakness is that it sits in committee with no movement, so its promise remains untested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: The bill's entire action history is two steps: it was introduced on February 26, 2025, and read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action has been recorded since the referral.
It has one cosponsor, Republican Senator Susan Collins, who joined Booker as an original sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has gained or lost anything; the people it would protect are still without the federal protection it offers, and employers with restrictive grooming policies continue under current law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; protections not enacted

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CROWN Act in the Senate on February 26, 2025.

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor, making it a bipartisan pair of sponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has only two senators attached so far, one Democrat and one Republican, and no vote has occurred, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Employers with grooming and appearance policies
industries.note: Businesses could no longer enforce rules that bar natural or protective hairstyles, and would face discrimination claims if they did; most employers are unaffected, but those with broad 'professional appearance' standards would need to change them. For workers, that means a hairstyle can no longer cost them a job.
The Fair Housing Act's enforcement machinery would apply to hair-based discrimination in housing; the practical effect is small but makes appearance-based screening explicitly challengeable.

industries.industry: Schools and institutions receiving federal funds
industries.note: Programs and schools receiving federal money could not penalize students for natural hairstyles without risking loss of compliance with civil rights rules; this mainly affects schools with dress codes targeting braids or locs.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the Judiciary Committee without a hearing or markup since February 2025. Most Senate bills referred to committee never reach a floor vote, and with only one cosponsor and no recorded committee action, its realistic path forward would require the committee to schedule work on it or a broader vehicle to carry its language.
